findings.source_passage: such attractions as are by no means unusual in children of two or three years old; an imperfect articulation, an earnest desire of having his own way, many cunning tricks, and a great deal of noise
findings.source_locator: paragraph 3, describing the child who supplanted the Dashwood daughters
findings.why_it_matters: This is Austen's sharpest and most celebrated ironic aside in the chapter — the satirical enumeration of infantile charms that outweighed years of devoted niece-service is a textbook example of her voice and is critically canonical. Its erasure removes the chapter's primary moment of Austenian wit.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the satirical catalogue verbatim or near-verbatim: 'an imperfect articulation, an earnest desire of having his own way, many cunning tricks, and a great deal of noise' — this is non-negotiable signature prose.

findings.source_passage: Yes, he would give them three thousand pounds: it would be liberal and handsome! It would be enough to make them completely easy. Three thousand pounds! he could spare so considerable a sum with little inconvenience.
findings.why_it_matters: The free indirect discourse rendering of John Dashwood's self-congratulatory generosity is interpretively central — it establishes his comic self-deception and sets up the famous deliberation scene that follows. The draft reduces this to a bare fact ('meditated the liberal present of a thousand pounds a-piece'), erasing the voice entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum the quoted interior monologue — 'Yes, he would give them three thousand pounds… he could spare so considerable a sum with little inconvenience' — as this free indirect speech is the chapter's principal comic register-marker.

findings.source_passage: it was a knowledge which her mother had yet to learn; and which one of her sisters had resolved never to be taught.
findings.why_it_matters: This closing epigram on knowing how to govern one's feelings is the sharpest formulation of the novel's central thematic opposition between the sisters; it also characterises Marianne with elegant economy before she is even individually described. Its omission flattens a passage of significant interpretive weight.
findings.suggested_fix: Append the sentence to the Elinor description: 'it was a knowledge which her mother had yet to learn; and which one of her sisters had resolved never to be taught.'

findings.source_passage: They gave themselves up wholly to their sorrow, seeking increase of wretchedness in every reflection that could afford it, and resolved against ever admitting consolation in future.
findings.source_locator: paragraph on Mrs. Dashwood and Marianne's grief
findings.why_it_matters: The draft ('renewed by choice, and heightened by every painful recollection; they resolved against consolation') preserves the bare fact but loses the specific ironic formulation — 'seeking increase of wretchedness' and 'every reflection that could afford it' — which defines Austen's satirical attitude toward excessive sensibility.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'seeking increase of wretchedness in every reflection that could afford it' — these particular phrases carry the ironic edge that establishes the novel's critique of sensibility.

findings.source_passage: He was not an ill-disposed young man, unless to be rather cold hearted and rather selfish is to be ill-disposed
findings.why_it_matters: The draft reproduces this phrase correctly. However, the surrounding ironic elaboration — 'he was, in general, well respected; for he conducted himself with propriety in the discharge of his ordinary duties' — is a further unit of Austenian irony that is present only in skeleton form in the draft, losing the deadpan 'ordinary duties' framing.
findings.suggested_fix: Minor: retain 'in the discharge of his ordinary duties' to preserve the ironic precision of the original.

summary: The draft commits two high-severity failures: erasure of the ironic catalogue of infant charms (Austen's most famous satirical set-piece in this chapter) and suppression of John Dashwood's self-congratulatory interior monologue (the chapter's principal instance of free indirect discourse), plus two medium-severity voice-flattenings.
